BOUNDARY TREES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · 123 Main St., Fresno, CA 93701

PURPOSE AND PARTIES: BOUNDARY TREES
Jordan Lee, the owner of the real property located at 123 Main St., Fresno, CA 93701 ("Party One"), and Morgan Casey, the owner of the adjoining real property located at 125 Main St., Fresno, CA 93701 ("Party Two"), are owners of adjoining parcels of real property in Fresno County, California. This document concerns the following tree or trees: 40-year-old Monterey pine, trunk appears to stand within a few feet of the rear property line.

This document states facts about California law addressing who owns a tree growing on or near the boundary between two adjoining properties, the circumstances under which an adjoining landowner may trim back branches or roots that cross onto that landowner's own property, and the civil penalty California's Civil Code imposes for a wrongful injury to another's timber, trees, or underwood. It draws on Civil Code Sections 833, 834, and 3346, and on a published California Court of Appeal decision, Booska v. Patel (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1786, that discusses the scope of a landowner's right to trim encroaching growth. This document states facts about that law; it does not tell Party One or Party Two what to do about the specific tree or trees described above, and it does not evaluate whether either party's conduct toward those trees is or was reasonable, authorized, or a trespass.

OWNERSHIP OF A TREE WHOSE TRUNK STANDS WHOLLY ON ONE OWNER'S LAND
California's Civil Code states a rule for trees whose trunk stands entirely within the boundary of a single owner's land: that owner owns the tree exclusively, even though the tree's roots may grow into a neighboring owner's land. The statute expresses this as a rule of exclusive ownership tied to the location of the trunk specifically, not the roots or any overhanging branches. This section has not been amended since its original enactment in 1872, and its text still uses the gender-specific pronoun "him" from that original enactment rather than gender-neutral language.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Trees whose trunks stand wholly upon the land of one owner belong exclusively to him, although their roots grow into the land of another."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 833, California Civil Code, ownership of a tree whose trunk stands wholly on one owner's land (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=833.)
  Known gap: Civil Code Section 833 is a single, one-sentence statute; its fetched text does not itself define what counts as a tree's "trunk," does not address a trunk that grows across a boundary line rather than standing wholly on one side of it (a circumstance the companion statute quoted in this document's next clause, Section 834, separately addresses), and does not itself state any remedy for wrongful injury to a tree it identifies as belonging to one owner (a separate topic addressed by Civil Code Section 3346, quoted elsewhere in this document). This clause states only what the statute's text says about ownership; it does not evaluate whether a specific tree's trunk in fact stands wholly on one side of a specific boundary.

COMMON OWNERSHIP OF A TREE STANDING ON THE BOUNDARY ITSELF
A separate, adjoining Civil Code section addresses a different situation from the one described in this document's preceding clause: a tree whose trunk stands partly on the land of two or more adjoining ("coterminous") owners. For that situation, the statute states that the tree belongs to those owners in common, rather than exclusively to either one of them. A published California Court of Appeal decision, Booska v. Patel, later described this same basic distinction in its own words while resolving an unrelated dispute about root-cutting, characterizing boundary-line trees as "jointly owned by the neighbors" and contrasting that with a tree whose trunk stands solely on one owner's property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Trees whose trunks stand partly on the land of two or more coterminous owners, belong to them in common."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 834, California Civil Code, common ownership of a tree whose trunk stands on the boundary between two or more owners' land (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=834.)
  "Patel notes a difference in the legal treatment of trees growing on a boundary line and trees entirely on the property of one owner which overhang the property of another. The only difference, however, seems to be that the boundary line trees are deemed to be jointly owned by the neighbors, while the tree with a trunk solely on the property of one belongs to that one."
  — Booska v. Patel (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1786, 1791, fn. 4, California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, describing the boundary-tree/solely-owned-tree distinction (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263644/booska-v-patel/)
  Known gap: Civil Code Section 834's text states that a boundary-line tree belongs to the coterminous owners "in common" but does not itself specify the proportion of that common ownership (for example, whether it is necessarily equal between two owners, or apportioned some other way), and does not define "coterminous." The Booska v. Patel passage quoted here is the Court of Appeal's own paraphrase of a distinction it attributes to two older cases, Anderson v. Weiland (1936) 12 Cal.App.2d 730 and Scarborough v. Woodill (1907) 7 Cal.App. 39; neither of those two older cases was independently fetched or verified in this research, and Booska's own opinion text does not cite Civil Code Section 833 or Section 834 by number — this document treats the Booska passage as case-law corroboration of the same substantive distinction the statute draws, using different wording ("jointly owned" rather than the statute's "belong to them in common"), not as a citation to either statute. This clause does not evaluate whether a specific tree's trunk in fact stands on a boundary line.

THE RIGHT TO TRIM ENCROACHING BRANCHES OR ROOTS, AND ITS LIMITS
In Booska v. Patel, the California Court of Appeal addressed a dispute in which one landowner had hired a contractor to sever the roots of a neighbor's tree that had grown into his yard, and the trial court had granted the landowner summary judgment on the theory that landowners have an unqualified, absolute right to sever any encroaching roots from their own property. The Court of Appeal described the origin of that "absolute right" language in an earlier case, Bonde v. Bishop (1952) 112 Cal.App.2d 1, which had stated that a landowner may remove encroaching portions of a neighbor's tree whether or not they cause damage, without first needing to sue and prove the encroachment is a nuisance. But the Booska court held that this right is not unlimited: after reviewing secondary authorities and other California cases addressing a landowner's duty to manage property reasonably, the court concluded that a landowner's rights in managing tree roots or branches on the landowner's own property are tempered by a duty to act reasonably, and it reversed the summary judgment because triable issues of fact existed about whether the specific conduct at issue had been reasonable.

  — Booska v. Patel (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1786, 1789, quoting Bonde v. Bishop (1952) 112 Cal.App.2d 1, 6, California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, on the scope of the right to remove encroaching tree growth (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263644/booska-v-patel/)
  "Thus, whatever rights Patel has in the management of his own land, those rights are tempered by his duty to act reasonably."
  — Booska v. Patel (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1786, 1791, California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, holding the right to manage encroaching growth is tempered by a duty of reasonableness (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263644/booska-v-patel/)

Patel is a published Court of Appeal (First Appellate District) decision; its own closing lines state that a petition for rehearing was denied and that the California Supreme Court denied a petition for review, meaning the decision became final without merits review by the Supreme Court. Booska reversed a summary judgment because triable issues of fact existed; it did not itself decide whether the defendant's actual conduct was or was not reasonable, and it does not state a numeric or bright-line test for what counts as reasonable management of encroaching roots or branches. The quoted "absolute right" language is Booska's own quotation of the earlier case Bonde v. Bishop (1952) 112 Cal.App.2d 1, 6; Bonde itself was not independently fetched or verified in this research, only Booska's verbatim quotation of it as it appears within Booska's own fetched opinion text. A CO-OWNER'S LIMITS REGARDING A JOINTLY OWNED BOUNDARY TREE
Booska v. Patel's discussion of boundary-line trees, described elsewhere in this document, continues with a further point drawn from two older California cases: because a boundary-line tree is jointly owned by the adjoining owners, one of those co-owners does not have the unilateral right to destroy the tree. The Court of Appeal described this as subject to a duty on each of the joint owners to use their own part of the tree in a way that does not unreasonably injure or destroy the whole of it.

  — Booska v. Patel (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1786, 1791, fn. 4, California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, on a co-owner's lack of unilateral right to destroy a jointly owned boundary tree (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2263644/booska-v-patel/)
  "so use his part as not unreasonably to injure or destroy the whole"
  — Booska v. Patel (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1786, 1791, fn. 4, quoting Anderson v. Weiland (1936) 12 Cal.App.2d 730 and Scarborough v. TREBLE AND DOUBLE DAMAGES FOR WRONGFUL INJURY TO TREES, AND THE FIVE-YEAR LIMITATIONS PERIOD
California's Civil Code sets a specific, elevated measure of damages for a wrongful injury to "timber, trees, or underwood" on another person's land, or the wrongful removal of it. As a default rule, the statute sets the measure of damages at three times the sum that would compensate for the actual detriment. The statute reduces that multiplier in two specified situations: to twice the actual detriment where the trespass was casual or involuntary, or where the defendant had probable cause to believe the land was the defendant's own (or the land of a person the defendant was acting for); and, in a narrower situation involving wood taken by highway officers to repair a public highway or bridge, to a sum equal to the actual detriment only, with no multiplier. The same statute separately states that an action for these damages must be commenced within five years from the date of the trespass.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3346(a), California Civil Code, measure of damages for wrongful injury to timber, trees, or underwood (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3346.)
  "Any action for the damages specified by subdivisions (a) and (b) of this section must be commenced within five years from the date of the trespass."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3346(c), California Civil Code, five-year limitations period for damages under this section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3346.)

Section 3346(a) applies to "timber, trees, or underwood" generally; its own text is not limited to boundary trees specifically and does not cross-reference Civil Code Sections 833 or 834, and its own text does not define "wrongful" or address how it interacts with the encroachment-trimming right described elsewhere in this document. REDUCED DAMAGES WHERE A TRESPASS RELIED ON A LICENSED BOUNDARY SURVEY
Civil Code Section 3346 states a further, separate exception from the treble- or double-damages measure described elsewhere in this document. Where a trespass onto another's land (including a trespass injuring trees) was committed in reliance on a survey of boundary lines that improperly fixed the location of a boundary, the statute limits the measure of damages to the actual detriment incurred, but only if two specific conditions both exist: the trespass must have been committed by a defendant who either personally procured the survey, or whose principal, lessor, or immediate predecessor in title procured it; and the survey itself must have been made by a person licensed under California law to practice land surveying.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The measure of damages to be assessed against a defendant for any trespass committed while acting in reliance upon a survey of boundary lines which improperly fixes the location of a boundary line, shall be the actual detriment incurred if both of the following conditions exist:(1) The trespass was committed by a defendant who either himself procured, or whose principal, lessor, or immediate predecessor in title procured the survey to be made; and(2) The survey was made by a person licensed under the laws of this State to practice land surveying."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3346(b), California Civil Code, reduced damages where a trespass relied on a licensed boundary survey (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3346.)

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code Section 3346 states a further, separate exception from the treble- or double-damages measure described elsewhere in this document. Where a trespass onto another's land (including a trespass injuring trees) was committed in reliance on a survey of boundary lines that improperly fixed the location of a boundary, the statute limits the measure of damages to the actual detriment incurred, but only if two specific conditions both exist: the trespass must have been committed by a defendant who either personally procured the survey, or whose principal, lessor, or immediate predecessor in title procured it; and the survey itself must have been made by a person licensed under California law to practice land surveying.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, reduced damages where a trespass relied on a licensed boundary survey
citations.quote: The measure of damages to be assessed against a defendant for any trespass committed while acting in reliance upon a survey of boundary lines which improperly fixes the location of a boundary line, shall be the actual detriment incurred if both of the following conditions exist:(1) The trespass was committed by a defendant who either himself procured, or whose principal, lessor, or immediate predecessor in title procured the survey to be made; and(2) The survey was made by a person licensed under the laws of this State to practice land surveying.
